extracted.intended_audience: trademark attorneys and practitioners who represent clients before the USPTO (and USPTO enrollment/discipline stakeholders)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and disciplinary requirements governing attorneys who represent trademark applicants before the USPTO, with emphasis on electronic signature rules, supervision of non-practitioners, candor to the Office, client communications, and corrective/remedial duties. Also describes sanctions and conditions for reinstatement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic signature must be personally entered by the named signatory
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO trademark signature rules require that all signatures be personally entered by the named signatory and that a person electronically signing a document must personally enter any combination of letters, numbers, spaces, and/or punctuation marks that he or she has adopted as a signature, placed between two forward slash ("/") symbols in the signature block on the electronic submission. See 37 C.F.R. §§ 2.193(a) and (c) and 37 C.F.R. § 11.18(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TMEP § 611.01(c) explains: "All documents must be personally signed... The person(s) identified as the signatory must manually enter the elements of the electronic signature. Another person (e.g., paralegal, legal assistant, or secretary) may not sign the name of a qualified practitioner or other authorized signatory. Just as signing the name of another person on paper does not serve as the signature of the person whose name is written, typing the electronic signature of another person is not a valid signature by that person."

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner must provide competent representation (37 C.F.R. § 11.101)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall provide competent representation to clients; incompetence includes failing to know and understand relevant USPTO trademark signature rules which results in violations of those rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competent representation encompasses understanding applicable USPTO rules (e.g., signature regulations) and ensuring filings comply; lack of such understanding can form the basis of professional discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act with reasonable diligence and promptness (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner shall act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client; failure to take reasonable steps to ensure clients' trademark filings were signed in accordance with USPTO trademark signature rules violates this duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes taking reasonable steps to ensure proper signing, monitoring filings and status, and timely remedial action when problems are discovered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communications with clients — keep clients informed and explain matters (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.104(a),(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must reasonably consult with clients about means to accomplish objectives, keep clients reasonably informed about the status of their matters, and explain matters to the extent reasonably necessary to permit clients to make informed decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically includes informing clients about actual or potential adverse consequences of not complying with USPTO trademark signature rules (e.g., whether an electronic signature by someone other than the named signatory jeopardizes intellectual property rights).

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-party payments — informed consent and no interference (37 C.F.R. § 11.108(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not accept compensation for representing a client from one other than the client unless, inter alia, the client gives informed consent and there is no interference with the practitioner's independence or professional judgment or with the client-practitioner relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioner must communicate to clients adequate information about material risks and reasonably available alternatives when a third party (e.g., a vendor) pays the attorney, and ensure independence of judgment is preserved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervision of non-practitioner assistants (37 C.F.R. § 11.503(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: When delegating tasks to non-practitioner paraprofessionals and other non-practitioner assistants, the practitioner must adequately supervise them, including giving appropriate instruction and monitoring their activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practitioner may be disciplined for failing to take reasonable steps to supervise paraprofessionals; must ensure their conduct is compatible with the practitioner's professional obligations (e.g., that they do not impermissibly sign documents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assist unauthorized practice of law (37 C.F.R. § 11.505)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not assist another to practice law in a jurisdiction in violation of the regulation of the legal profession in that jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorizing or instructing a non-practitioner to sign the practitioner's name on USPTO filings can constitute assisting unauthorized practice and is actionable under this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candor toward the USPTO; remedial duties when falsity or fraud is discovered (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.303(a)(1),(a)(3),(b),(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners shall not knowingly make a false statement of fact or law to a tribunal (the USPTO) or fail to correct a false statement previously made; if the practitioner comes to know of the falsity of material evidence, they shall take reasonable remedial measures, including, if necessary, disclosure to the USPTO. Practitioners must also disclose fraudulent conduct relating to an application or renewal and take reasonable remedial measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compliance may require disclosure to the USPTO even if such disclosure would otherwise implicate information protected under other rules. Examples include informing the Office when a filing or declaration was impermissibly signed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners shall not engage in conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice, which includes authorizing non-practitioners to sign the practitioner's name on trademark documents (including declarations) where the practitioner is the named signatory and attorney of record, with knowledge that the USPTO will rely on such documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing impermissibly signed applications can adversely affect the integrity of the trademark registration process and may render resulting registrations invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not file or permit filing of trademark applications/declarations not signed by named signatory
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners representing trademark applicants before the USPTO are reasonably expected not to file, or allow to be filed, trademark applications and declarations that are not signed by the named signatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trademark filings bearing invalid/impermissible signatures (e.g., TEAS Plus Application, Statement of Use, Combined Declaration of Use and Incontestability) are relied upon by the USPTO; improper signatures jeopardize registration integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor and control client contact points and correspondence (monitor USPTO correspondence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must monitor the status of trademark applications and any email addresses or points of contact provided to the USPTO for correspondence; reliance on a third party to provide relevant updates without monitoring is a failure of duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including a vendor-controlled email address in an application and failing to monitor it (so that USPTO correspondence goes unreviewed) can constitute lack of reasonable diligence and lead to discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct conflicts checks for clients represented before the Office
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must conduct conflicts checks with respect to work for different clients; failing to perform such checks violates professional obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In multi-client/vendor arrangements, the duty to identify conflicts remains with the practitioner even if clients are referred through a third party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to inform clients about impermissible signatures and advise potential consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: When impermissible signatures are discovered, the practitioner must personally apprise clients about the issue and advise them of the potential adverse consequences to their intellectual property rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order requires the respondent to contact each affected client and explain how the impermissible signing may affect pending applications and issued/renewed registrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to notify the USPTO's Office of Trademark Operations of impermissible signatures
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must inform the USPTO's Office of Trademark Operations of any impermissible signatures in filings for which the practitioner has been attorney of record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The agreed remediation required the respondent to inform the Office of Trademark Operations of all impermissible signatures and to provide supporting evidence of doing so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable remedial measures upon discovery of misconduct (including disclosure even if otherwise protected)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a practitioner has offered material evidence and then knows of its falsity or learns of fraudulent conduct related to examination of an application, the practitioner shall take reasonable remedial measures, which may include disclosure to the USPTO despite other confidentiality limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 37 C.F.R. § 11.303(d) and related commentary indicate disclosure obligations can override other privileges when rectifying material falsity or fraud before the USPTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreed sanctions and conditions for reinstatement and compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctions for the respondent include suspension from practice before the USPTO for three months, compliance with 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.58 and 11.60, provision of sworn affidavits/verified declarations within specified timeframes, a 21-month probationary period upon reinstatement, completion of six (6) hours of CLE on ethics/professional responsibility, and thorough review of TMEP provisions and specified regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific remedial requirements: within three months provide affidavits demonstrating (1) clients were informed about impermissible signatures and advised of consequences, (2) the Office of Trademark Operations was informed of impermissible signatures, and (3) signature practice since Oct 2020 ensures compliance; within 30 days provide Final Order to practitioner colleagues; before probation end provide CLE and attest to review of TMEP, 37 C.F.R. § 2.11, and commentary at 84 FR 31498-01. Failure to comply may trigger an Order to Show Cause and additional suspension.

rubrics_metrics.name: OED enforcement process for probation violations (Order to Show Cause; possible additional suspension)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the OED Director believes the respondent failed to comply with the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct or probation conditions, OED shall issue an Order to Show Cause, provide notice and an opportunity to respond, and may request the USPTO Director to impose an immediate suspension for the balance of the probation or an additional nine months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order to Show Cause is sent to respondent's last address of record and grants 15 days to respond; OED may supply arguments/evidence to the USPTO Director seeking further discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited recognition to practice for narrow compliance purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent was granted limited recognition to practice before the Office beginning on the date of the Final Order and expiring sixty (60) days after that date solely to facilitate compliance with 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.58(b) and 11.303.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limited recognition is narrowly tailored to allow the respondent to take actions necessary to comply with immediate remediation obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and public notice of disciplinary final orders
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director shall electronically publish the Final Order at OED's FOIA Reading Room and publish a materially consistent notice in the Official Gazette describing the suspension/probation and the conduct underlying it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication explains the factual basis and relevant regulations violated and serves as public notice and precedent for future disciplinary considerations.
